name: J F Mitchell Airport
before:
Bequia's airport, and the reason the island is reachable at all without a boat. Until it opened in 1992 Bequia could only be reached by sea, which was the single biggest constraint on tourism here.

It is small and honest about it. This is a turboprop field for scheduled and charter work, with small private jets also using it, and there are no air bridges, so passengers walk to the aircraft. Most flights are domestic within Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, with around ten international services a week from Barbados and Saint Lucia.

The airport sits on reclaimed land at Paget Farm, built after a 1986 feasibility study recommended a runway of 850 metres with room to extend. It is the third largest airport by area in the country, behind Argyle and Canouan.

It is named after Sir James Fitz-Allen Mitchell, Premier and then Prime Minister of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
after:
Bequia's only airport, opened in 1992. The alternative is the ferry from Kingstown on St Vincent.

It is small, with one runway of 1,100 metres, used by small propeller aircraft on scheduled and charter flights and by private aircraft. SVG Air's scheduled flights link it with Barbados, St Vincent, Canouan, Union Island and Grenada. Charter flights also come in from St Lucia.

claims.inAfter: SVG Air's scheduled flights link it with Barbados, St Vincent, Canouan, Union Island and Grenada.
claims.note: Replaces 'Most flights are domestic ... with around ten international services a week from Barbados and Saint Lucia' (cuts below). The Bequia Tourism Association says the airport has daily scheduled flights to and from Barbados and scheduled flights to Grenada (SVG Air), Union Island, Canouan and St Vincent; SVG Air's own page lists daily flights to and from all of these places, and the association's page gives SVG Air a Barbados reservations number. The association is the island's tourism body, a lower tier than an airline or a government, but SVG Air's own page lists the same places.

claims.why: The 1992 opening is kept (two sources). 'Could only be reached by sea' before then rests on Wikipedia alone; the tourism association and Sir James Mitchell's letter do not say it.

claims.claim: the single biggest constraint on tourism
claims.wasBefore: which was the single biggest constraint on tourism here
claims.why: Overstated. Wikipedia says the lack of an airstrip was 'a major constraint to tourism development', and Sir James Mitchell's 2016 letter that without the airport the hotel and villa investment 'would never have been attracted'; neither says single biggest.

claims.why: A judgement with no source; replaced by the runway length, which shows how small it is.

claims.why: Disputed. Wikipedia says small private jets fly here, but Sir James Mitchell's 2016 letter says another 100 metres of runway would 'provide accommodation for private jets'. Softened to private aircraft, which SVG Air handles here.

claims.wasBefore: and there are no air bridges, so passengers walk to the aircraft

claims.claim: around ten international services a week from Barbados and Saint Lucia
claims.wasBefore: with around ten international services a week from Barbados and Saint Lucia
claims.why: A weekly count on Wikipedia alone, undated, with no airport count to replace it (the airport has no site of its own). Barbados and St Lucia are kept, as scheduled flights and charters respectively.

claims.claim: on reclaimed land at Paget Farm
claims.wasBefore: The airport sits on reclaimed land at Paget Farm
claims.why: Not independently confirmed. Wikipedia's lead and infobox place it on reclaimed land at Paget Farm; the only other source, Sir James Mitchell's 2016 letter, mentions a 1974 design 'for a 4,000-foot runway at Paget Farm' and 'dredged sand', but Wikipedia's History copies that letter, so the two are not clearly independent. Worth restoring if a government or survey source can be read.

claims.claim: a 1986 feasibility study recommended 850 metres with room to extend
claims.wasBefore: built after a 1986 feasibility study recommended a runway of 850 metres with room to extend
claims.why: Wikipedia alone, and out of date as a description: the runway built is 1,100 m (kept above). The 2016 letter dates the studies to 1985 (financing) and 1987 (final study).

claims.claim: third largest airport by area, behind Argyle and Canouan
claims.wasBefore: It is the third largest airport by area in the country, behind Argyle and Canouan.
claims.why: 'By area' rests on Wikipedia alone. OurAirports' runway lengths put it third too (after Argyle and Canouan), but that is a different measure, so the runway length is given instead.

claims.claim: named after Sir James Fitz-Allen Mitchell
claims.wasBefore: It is named after Sir James Fitz-Allen Mitchell, Premier and then Prime Minister of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone, and unreferenced there. No saved source says whom the airport is named after: Sir James Mitchell's own 2016 letter about the airport does not mention its name, and the Bequia Tourism Association's history page names an earlier James Fitz Allen Mitchell, a boat-builder, without mentioning the airport. Worth restoring when a second source is found.

claims.claim: departure tax paid at the airport on local airlines
claims.why: Held back: new, and on the Bequia Tourism Association's page alone, but possibly the most useful line for an agent. It says there is a national departure tax of EC$100 (about US$40), included in the ticket on major airlines out of Argyle, but paid on departure by passengers flying SVG Air, GAA or Mustique Airways out of Bequia and the other Grenadine airports.
